claim: During spatial navigation, animals use self-motion to estimate positions through path integration.
source: During spatial navigation, animals use self-motion to estimate positions through path integration.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus about animal navigation.

claim: Estimation errors accumulate over time during path integration.
source: However, estimation errors accumulate over time and it is unclear how they are corrected.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus about path integration.

claim: Individual cue cells exhibited firing fields only near visual cues during virtual navigation.
source: During virtual navigation, individual cue cells exhibited firing fields only near visual cues and their population response formed sequences repeated at each cue.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including raster plots and spatial firing rates shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The population response of cue cells formed sequences repeated at each cue.
source: During virtual navigation, individual cue cells exhibited firing fields only near visual cues and their population response formed sequences repeated at each cue.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 4.

claim: Cue cells consistently responded to cues across multiple environments.
source: These cells consistently responded to cues across multiple environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: On a track with cues on left and right sides, most cue cells only responded to cues on one side.
source: On a track with cues on left and right sides, most cue cells only responded to cues on one side.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: During navigation in a real arena, cue cells showed spatially stable activity.
source: During navigation in a real arena, they showed spatially stable activity and accounted for 32% of unidentified, spatially stable MEC cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Cue cells accounted for 32% of unidentified, spatially stable MEC cells.
source: During navigation in a real arena, they showed spatially stable activity and accounted for 32% of unidentified, spatially stable MEC cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: Cue cells could provide spatial information for error correction during path integration.
source: These cue cell properties demonstrate that the MEC contains a code representing spatial landmarks, which could be important for error correction during path integration.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the properties of cue cells observed in the study.

claim: Animals navigate using landmarks, objects or features that provide sensory cues, to estimate spatial location.
source: Animals navigate using landmarks, objects or features that provide sensory cues, to estimate spatial location.
evidence: This is a statement that draws from established scientific consensus about animal navigation.

claim: When sensory cues defining position are either absent or unreliable during navigation, many animals can use self-motion to update internal representations of location through path integration (Mittelstaedt, 1982; Tsoar et al., 2011).
source: When sensory cues defining position are either absent or unreliable during navigation, many animals can use self-motion to update internal representations of location through path integration (Mittelstaedt, 1982; Tsoar et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A set of interacting brain regions, including the entorhinal cortex, parietal cortex, and the hippocampus participate in path integration.
source: A set of interacting brain regions, including the entorhinal cortex, parietal cortex, and the hippocampus (Brun et al., 2008; Bush et al., 2015; Calton et al., 2003; Calton et al., 2008; Clark et al., 2010; Clark et al., 2013; Clark et al., 2009; Clark and Taube, 2009; Frohardt et al., 2006; Geva-Sagiv et al., 2015; Golob and Taube, 1999; Golob et al., 1998; Hollup et al., 2001; Moser et al., 1993; Parron et al., 2004; Parron and Save, 2004; Taube et al., 1992; Whitlock et al., 2008) participate in this process.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Grid cells in the MEC have multiple firing fields arrayed in a triangular lattice that tile an environment (Hafting et al., 2005).
source: Grid cells in the MEC have multiple firing fields arrayed in a triangular lattice that tile an environment (Hafting et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Grid cell firing pattern is observed across different environments with the grid cell population activity coherently shifting during locomotion (Fyhn et al., 2007).
source: This firing pattern is observed across different environments with the grid cell population activity coherently shifting during locomotion (Fyhn et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Grid cells form a spatial metric used by a path integrator.
source: These observations have led to the hypothesis that grid cells form a spatial metric used by a path integrator.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on observations from previous research.

claim: Theoretical studies have demonstrated how velocity-encoding inputs to grid cell circuits could shift grid cell firing patterns, as expected of a path integrator (Barry and Burgess, 2014; Burak and Fiete, 2009; Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; McNaughton et al., 2006).
source: Given this, theoretical studies have demonstrated how velocity-encoding inputs to grid cell circuits could shift grid cell firing patterns, as expected of a path integrator (Barry and Burgess, 2014; Burak and Fiete, 2009; Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; McNaughton et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical research.

claim: Cells encoding the speed of locomotion have been identified in the MEC (Kropff et al., 2015).
source: Cells encoding the speed of locomotion have been identified in this region (Kropff et al., 2015), providing evidence of velocity-encoding inputs and further support for the role of MEC in path integration.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A solution to the problem of error accumulation in path integration is to use reliable spatial cues to correct estimates of position (Evans et al., 2016; Hardcastle et al., 2015; Pollock et al., 2018).
source: A solution to this problem is to use reliable spatial cues to correct estimates of position (Evans et al., 2016; Hardcastle et al., 2015; Pollock et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The absence of visual landmarks significantly disrupted grid cell firing patterns (Chen et al., 2016; Pérez-Escobar et al., 2016).
source: For example, the absence of visual landmarks significantly disrupted grid cell firing patterns (Chen et al., 2016; Pérez-Escobar et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Experiments that maintained the boundaries of a one-dimensional environment but manipulated nonmetric visual cues caused rate changes in grid cells (Pérez-Escobar et al., 2016).
source: Also, experiments that maintained the boundaries of a one-dimensional environment but manipulated nonmetric visual cues caused rate changes in grid cells (Pérez-Escobar et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The decoupling of an animal's self-motion and visual scene altered grid cell firing patterns (Campbell et al., 2018).
source: The decoupling of an animal's self-motion and visual scene altered grid cell firing patterns (Campbell et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Grid cell firing patterns were influenced by nearby boundaries (Carpenter et al., 2015; Derdikman et al., 2009; Giocomo, 2016; Hardcastle et al., 2015; Krupic et al., 2015; Krupic et al., 2018; Stensola et al., 2015; Yamahachi et al., 2013).
source: Finally, many studies have shown that grid cell firing patterns were influenced by nearby boundaries (Carpenter et al., 2015; Derdikman et al., 2009; Giocomo, 2016; Hardcastle et al., 2015; Krupic et al., 2015; Krupic et al., 2018; Stensola et al., 2015; Yamahachi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Border cells in the MEC have firing fields extending across environmental boundaries (Solstad et al., 2008).
source: Border cells in the MEC, with firing fields extending across environmental boundaries (Solstad et al., 2008), are good candidates for supplying information for error correction near the perimeter of simple arenas (Pollock et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Border cells are good candidates for supplying information for error correction near the perimeter of simple arenas (Pollock et al., 2018).
source: Border cells in the MEC, with firing fields extending across environmental boundaries (Solstad et al., 2008), are good candidates for supplying information for error correction near the perimeter of simple arenas (Pollock et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: An animal's interactions with boundaries yielded direction-dependent error correction (Hardcastle et al., 2015).
source: This role of border cells is supported by the fact that an animal's interactions with boundaries yielded direction-dependent error correction (Hardcastle et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Grid cell firing fields are maintained throughout open arenas in locations where border cells are not active.
source: However, grid cell firing fields are maintained throughout open arenas in locations where border cells are not active and thus cannot participate in error correction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of grid cells and border cells.

claim: Border cells have been shown to respond to landmarks in virtual reality (Campbell et al., 2018).
source: In the MEC, while border cells have been shown to respond to landmarks in virtual reality (Campbell et al., 2018), increasing evidence suggests that unclassified cells also contain information about spatial environments (Diehl et al., 2017; Hardcastle et al., 2017; Høydal et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Increasing evidence suggests that unclassified cells in the MEC also contain information about spatial environments (Diehl et al., 2017; Hardcastle et al., 2017; Høydal et al., 2019).
source: In the MEC, while border cells have been shown to respond to landmarks in virtual reality (Campbell et al., 2018), increasing evidence suggests that unclassified cells also contain information about spatial environments (Diehl et al., 2017; Hardcastle et al., 2017; Høydal et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mice were trained to unidirectionally navigate along linear tracks in virtual reality to receive water rewards.
source: Mice were trained to unidirectionally navigate along linear tracks in virtual reality to receive water rewards.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Virtual tracks were 8 meters long.
source: Virtual tracks were 8 meters long and had a similar general organization and appearance: tracks began with a set of black walls, followed by a short segment with patterned walls, and then finally the majority of the track was comprised of a long corridor with a simple wall pattern (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: Different environments were defined by distinct pairs of identical visual cues (tower-like structures) symmetrically present along both sides of the corridor.
source: Different environments were defined by distinct pairs of identical visual cues (tower-like structures) symmetrically present along both sides of the corridor.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: The last cue was always associated with a water reward.
source: These cues were non-uniformly spaced along the track and the last cue was always associated with a water reward.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: 789 units were recorded in the MEC of three mice using tetrodes.
source: We used tetrodes to record 789 units in the MEC of three mice (Materials and methods and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data collected.

claim: A subpopulation of recorded units exhibited spiking occurring only near cue locations along the virtual linear tracks.
source: Activity of a subpopulation of these units exhibited a striking pattern, with spiking occurring only near cue locations along the virtual linear tracks (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Spatial firing fields were preferentially located near cue locations.
source: Prominent peaks in the spatial firing rate were present at cue locations. In order to classify these peaks, we defined spatial firing fields as the locations along the track where the spatial firing rate exceeded 70% of the shuffled data (Materials and Methods) and observed that the spatial firing fields were preferentially located near cue locations (fields indicated by red lines in Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Cells with cue scores above the threshold represented ~13% of all recorded cells.
source: Cells with cue scores above the threshold (95th percentile of shuffled data, Materials and Methods) represented ~13% of all recorded cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The mean firing field fraction for spatial bins of the firing field distribution in cue regions (0.4 ± 0.1) was higher than that for bins outside of cue regions (0.2 ± 0.1) (paired one-tailed t-test: fraction of cue cell population with fields located in cue region bins > fraction of cell population with fields in bins outside cue regions, N = 100, 3 animals, p=1.2 × 10−11).
source: The mean firing field fraction for spatial bins of the firing field distribution in cue regions (0.4 ± 0.1) was higher than that for bins outside of cue regions (0.2 ± 0.1) (paired one-tailed t-test: fraction of cue cell population with fields located in cue region bins > fraction of cell population with fields in bins outside cue regions, N = 100, 3 animals, p=1.2 × 10−11).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: At the beginning of both with-cues and missing-cues tracks, where the tracks were identical, the spatial firing rates of cue cells were similar across tracks.
source: At the beginning of both with-cues and missing-cues tracks, where the tracks were identical, the spatial firing rates of cue cells were similar across tracks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Spatial firing fields were prominent at cue locations along the entire remaining part of the with-cues track but were not present on the same part of the missing-cues track.
source: However, the firing patterns changed dramatically from the point along the track where the environments began to differ. Spatial firing fields were prominent at cue locations along the entire remaining part of the with-cues track (Figure 2A, top) but were not present on the same part of the missing-cues track (Figure 2A, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The correlation between the firing rate and template was lower for the firing rates on the missing cues track in Region B but not for region A (Figure 2B, paired one-tailed t-test: correlation in Region B on with-cues track > correlation in Region B on missing-cues track, N = 65, 3 animals, for region A: p=0.56; for region B: p=1×10−14).
source: This correlation was lower for the firing rates on the missing cues track in Region B but not for region A (Figure 2B, paired one-tailed t-test: correlation in Region B on with-cues track > correlation in Region B on missing-cues track, N = 65, 3 animals, for region A: p=0.56; for region B: p=1×10−14).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In Region B, the fraction of the region with spatial firing fields was lower in the missing-cues track compared to the with-cues track (Figure 2D, paired one-tailed t-test: field fraction on with-cues track > field fraction on missing-cues track, N = 65, 3 animals, for region A: p=1.00, for region B: p=0.0002).
source: In Region B, the fraction of the region with spatial firing fields was lower in the missing-cues track compared to the with-cues track (Figure 2D, paired one-tailed t-test: field fraction on with-cues track > field fraction on missing-cues track, N = 65, 3 animals, for region A: p=1.00, for region B: p=0.0002).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A small percentage of cue cells were conjunctive with border (11%) or grid (28%) cell types.
source: We found that a small percentage of cue cells were conjunctive with border (11%) or grid (28%) cell types, and some cue cells had a significant head direction score (35%) (since the head direction score is based on orientation tuning, we do not consider the head direction cell type to be a spatial cell type).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Some cue cells had a significant head direction score (35%).
source: We found that a small percentage of cue cells were conjunctive with border (11%) or grid (28%) cell types, and some cue cells had a significant head direction score (35%) (since the head direction score is based on orientation tuning, we do not consider the head direction cell type to be a spatial cell type).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The total percentage of cue cells (13%) in the dataset was comparable to that of grid and border cells.
source: The total percentage of cue cells (13%) in the dataset was comparable to that of grid and border cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Most cue cells (63%) were not conjunctive with a previously known spatial cell type.
source: Since most cue cells (63%) were not conjunctive with a previously known spatial cell type, we next examined their spatial activity patterns during navigation in the real arena.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The spatial firing patterns of cue cells in real arenas were irregular but surprisingly stable.
source: We calculated the spatial stability as the correlation between these two halves and found that the spatial firing patterns were irregular but surprisingly stable.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cue cells showed comparable spatial stability as other existing cell types.
source: In contrast, our newly classified cue cells showed comparable spatial stability as other existing cell types, supporting its ability to encode spatial information during navigation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Cue cells accounted for 7% of the population of spatially stable cells.
source: Cue cells accounted for 7% of the population of spatially stable cells, and for 14% of the previously unclassified spatially stable cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Cue cells accounted for 14% of the previously unclassified spatially stable cells.
source: Cue cells accounted for 7% of the population of spatially stable cells, and for 14% of the previously unclassified spatially stable cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Cue cells formed a sequence of spatial firing fields that was repeated at each cue.
source: We found a striking pattern where cue cells formed a sequence of spatial firing fields that was repeated at each cue.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The mean ridge/background ratio for cue cells (1.8) was higher than that for spatial field shuffled data (1.2 ± 0.35, p=9.8 × 10−7; N = 100 cue cells, Figure 4B).
source: We note that although ordering the spatial firing rates of the cells by their spatial shift was expected to create a ridge of firing rate along the diagonal, the mean ridge/background ratio for cue cells (1.8) was higher than that for spatial field shuffled data (1.2 ± 0.35, p=9.8 × 10−7; N = 100 cue cells, Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Most cue cells had small spatial shifts.
source: Most cue cells had small spatial shifts (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In layer 2 of the left MEC most cue cells only passed the threshold for either left or right template.
source: We found that in layer 2 of the left MEC most cue cells only passed the threshold for either left or right template.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There were 8.1% and 21.9% of cells uniquely identified as left and right cue cells, respectively.
source: There were 8.1% and 21.9% of cells uniquely identified as left and right cue cells, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Very few cells passed the thresholds of both templates (14 out of the total population of 281 left and right cells (5%), and 1.6% of the population of all cells, N = 4 animals, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
source: Very few cells passed the thresholds of both templates (14 out of the total population of 281 left and right cells (5%), and 1.6% of the population of all cells, N = 4 animals, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) and their responses correlated to the two single side cue templates under different spatial shifts (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), indicating that they did not simultaneously respond to both left and right cues.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The distribution of bilateral scores of left and right cells together was bimodal with two major peaks at large absolute values (Figure 5E).
source: We found that the distribution of bilateral scores of left and right cells together was bimodal with two major peaks at large absolute values (Figure 5E), suggesting that the left and right cue cells indeed responded to cues on one side of the track.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The percentages of left and right cue cells corresponding to the current templates were significantly higher than those to random templates (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
source: In contrast, we found that the percentages of left and right cue cells corresponding to the current templates were significantly higher than those to random templates (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), indicating that the locations of left and right cues were preferentially represented by cue cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The calcium responses of imaged left and right cue cells also had consistent spatial shifts to individual left and right cues, respectively, and the response together formed sequences (Figure 5D).
source: As observed for tetrode-recorded cue cells (Figure 4A), the calcium responses of imaged left and right cue cells also had consistent spatial shifts to individual left and right cues, respectively, and the response together formed sequences (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In the left MEC, there were more right cue cells than left cue cells (Figure 5F).
source: In the left MEC, there were more right cue cells than left cue cells (Figure 5F) and the cue scores of right cue cells were higher than those of left cue cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The cue scores of right cue cells were higher than those of left cue cells (Figure 5G).
source: In the left MEC, there were more right cue cells than left cue cells (Figure 5F) and the cue scores of right cue cells were higher than those of left cue cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Many cue cells maintained cue-correlated responses along both tracks (Figure 6A, N = 5 animals).
source: We found that many cue cells maintained cue-correlated responses along both tracks (Figure 6A, N = 5 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The percentages of cue cells and non-cue cells that remained as the same cell types on two different tracks were significantly higher than chance (Figure 6B).
source: In general, the percentages of cue cells and non-cue cells that remained as the same cell types on two different tracks were significantly higher than chance (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Cue cells showed highly correlated spatial shifts relative to cue templates across different tracks (Figure 6C).
source: Finally, cue cells showed highly correlated spatial shifts relative to cue templates across different tracks (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Cue cells are a functional cell type representing visual cue information across different environments.
source: These observations suggest that cue cells are a functional cell type representing visual cue information across different environments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Cue cells could provide a source of spatial information in the local circuits of MEC that could be used in error correction in landmark rich environments.
source: These properties of cue cells suggest that they could provide a source of spatial information in the local circuits of MEC that could be used in error correction in landmark rich environments.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the properties of cue cells observed in the study.

claim: Most cue cells were not grid or border cells, yet they did have noticeably stable, and somewhat irregular, spatial firing patterns in real arenas.
source: We found that most cue cells were not grid or border cells, yet they did have noticeably stable, and somewhat irregular, spatial firing patterns in real arenas.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Cue cells account for a significant fraction (~22%) of the previously unexplained spatially-stable cells in MEC.
source: Cue cells account for a significant fraction (~22%) of the previously unexplained spatially-stable cells in MEC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A vast majority of cue cells had some orientation tuning (35%).
source: While most cue cells were not grid or border cells, a vast majority of them had some orientation tuning (35%).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Place cells typically have only a single firing field during navigation along short linear tracks, even in virtual reality environments with prominent visual cues along the tracks (Dombeck et al., 2010).
source: Place cells typically have only a single firing field during navigation along short linear tracks, even in virtual reality environments with prominent visual cues along the tracks (Dombeck et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Boundary vector cells encode distance to a boundary (Lever et al., 2009; Stewart et al., 2014).
source: Boundary vector cells, which were found in subiculum, encode distance to a boundary (Lever et al., 2009; Stewart et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cue cells have properties distinct from both place cells and boundary vector cells.
source: Thus, cue cells have properties distinct from both place cells and boundary vector cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of cue cells with place cells and boundary vector cells.

claim: It is possible that cue cells could have properties similar to landmark vector cells found in the hippocampus (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2013).
source: It is possible that cue cells could have properties similar to landmark vector cells found in the hippocampus (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the properties of cue cells and a citation to previous research.

claim: A recent paper described a new cell type, termed object-vector cells (Høydal et al., 2019).
source: In particular, a recent paper described a new cell type, termed object-vector cells (Høydal et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Object-vector cells belong to a similar cell population as cue cells.
source: We believe these cells belong to a similar cell population as our cue cells do since there are some comparable findings on this cue-related cell type: Similar percentages of cue/object-vector cells; these cells are not predominately conjunctive with other spatial cell types; and these cells maintain cue-related firing across environments (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of cue cells with object-vector cells.

claim: Cue cells mostly responded to cues located on one side and the right cues were predominately represented in the left MEC.
source: Along with the sequential nature of the activity of these cells, we also specifically studied cue cells in layers 2 and 3 of the MEC and discovered the side-preference of these cells. The fact that these cells mostly responded to cues located on one side and that the right cues were predominately represented in the left MEC, strongly supported a visual input-based mechanism in driving cue cell response.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Grid cells are grouped into modules based on each cell's grid spacing.
source: Grid cells are grouped into modules based on each cell's grid spacing.
evidence: This is a statement that draws from established scientific consensus about grid cells.

claim: Each grid module maintains its own orientation, to which all grid cells align and are related by a two-dimensional spatial phase.
source: Each grid module maintains its own orientation, to which all grid cells align and are related by a two-dimensional spatial phase.
evidence: This is a statement that draws from established scientific consensus about grid cells.

claim: Grid cells in a given module maintain their relative spatial phase offsets across different environments (Fyhn et al., 2007), including linear tracks (Yoon et al., 2016).
source: Grid cells in a given module maintain their relative spatial phase offsets across different environments (Fyhn et al., 2007), including linear tracks (Yoon et al., 2016), indicating that the population of grid cells form a consistent spatial metric largely defined only by the two-dimensional phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The population of grid cells form a consistent spatial metric largely defined only by the two-dimensional phase.
source: Grid cells in a given module maintain their relative spatial phase offsets across different environments (Fyhn et al., 2007), including linear tracks (Yoon et al., 2016), indicating that the population of grid cells form a consistent spatial metric largely defined only by the two-dimensional phase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of grid cells.

claim: Grid cell dynamics are constrained to a two-dimensional attractor manifold (Yoon et al., 2013).
source: This provides support for the idea that grid cell dynamics are constrained to a two-dimensional attractor manifold (Yoon et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: One role of cue cells could be to act as external error-correction inputs to the path integrator network that tend to drive the neural activity pattern to manifold locations appropriate for each landmark.
source: One role could be to act as external error-correction inputs to the path integrator network that tend to drive the neural activity pattern to manifold locations appropriate for each landmark.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential functional role of cue cells.

claim: An analogous use was proposed for border cells, in which they contribute to error correction near boundaries (Hardcastle et al., 2015; Pollock et al., 2018).
source: An analogous use was proposed for border cells, in which they contribute to error correction near boundaries (Hardcastle et al., 2015; Pollock et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: An alternative role for cue cells in path integration would be to produce a continuous adjustment of location.
source: An alternative, or additional, role for cue cells in path integration would be to produce a continuous adjustment of location.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential functional role of cue cells.

claim: The sequence of activity that was produced across the cue cell population as individual landmarks were passed could drive the network activity continuously along the manifold.
source: The sequence of activity that was produced across the cue cell population as individual landmarks were passed could drive the network activity continuously along the manifold, in essence acting as a velocity input that is quite different from those traditionally considered, such as running speed.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential functional role of cue cells.

claim: The collective state of a line attractor can be moved continuously along the manifold by an appropriately learned sequence of external inputs (Hopfield, 2015; Ocko et al., 2018).
source: This use, as an effective velocity, is analogous to the recent demonstration (Hopfield, 2015; Ocko et al., 2018) that the collective state of a line attractor can be moved continuously along the manifold by an appropriately learned sequence of external inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In principle, both path-integration and error correction can be combined through this process.
source: In principle, both path-integration and error correction can be combined through this process.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential functional role of cue cells.

claim: Cue scores form a continuum.
source: Although our analysis and discussion of cue cells have largely followed the traditional approach of describing MEC cells according to discrete classes, it is interesting to note that cue scores, like grid, head direction, and border scores, each form a continuum and that a significant fraction of cells in MEC are conjunctive for more than one class (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an observation based on the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: A significant fraction of cells in MEC are conjunctive for more than one class (Figure 3).
source: Although our analysis and discussion of cue cells have largely followed the traditional approach of describing MEC cells according to discrete classes, it is interesting to note that cue scores, like grid, head direction, and border scores, each form a continuum and that a significant fraction of cells in MEC are conjunctive for more than one class (Figure 3).
